subject: Computer Networking
title: Single Sign-On
description: A short lesson to help you apply Single Sign-On.

hook.text: One login, access to everything: email, CRM, HR, cloud. SSO makes that seamless and secure.

buildup.text: SSO uses a central identity provider. When you log in once, it issues tokens for every connected application.

discovery.text: SAML and OIDC carry the identity assertion. The app trusts the identity provider instead of managing passwords.

twist.text: If the identity provider is breached, every connected app is exposed. SSO is a single point of convenience — and risk.

climax.text: That's why MFA on the identity provider is critical. Protecting that one login protects everything behind it.

punchline.text: SSO means one strong login replaces many weak ones.

quiz.question: What is the main risk of Single Sign-On?
options: A breach of the identity provider exposes all connected apps

details.summary: Single sign-on lets users authenticate once and gain access to multiple applications without logging in again. Protocols like SAML and OIDC enable SSO by establishing trust between identity providers and service providers.
details.whyItMatters: SSO reduces password sprawl, simplifies user experience, and gives organizations a single point to enforce security policies, enable MFA, and revoke access across all applications instantly.
takeaways: Users authenticate once and access multiple applications seamlessly
SAML and OpenID Connect are the dominant SSO protocols
Centralized authentication simplifies security policy enforcement

faq.question: How does SSO improve security?
faq.answer: SSO reduces the number of passwords users must remember, decreasing password reuse and phishing risk. MFA only needs to be configured once at the identity provider. When an employee leaves, disabling their SSO account instantly revokes access to all connected applications.

faq.question: What happens if the SSO provider goes down?
faq.answer: If the identity provider is unavailable, users cannot authenticate to any connected application. This makes SSO infrastructure a critical single point of failure.
